04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma reached the hire car she had collected after the train journey. Rain struck the windscreen hard enough to blur the Morrison house behind her. She left the engine off and placed her notebook on the passenger seat.

Nora’s account had given her a direction, but not an accusation. She had seen Claire get into a car. She associated a similar vehicle with the community hall and remembered a man called Reid standing beside it on another occasion. She could not identify the driver on the evening Claire vanished.

Emma read her notes again, checking where observation ended and assumption began. She had crossed out a sentence that described Reid as the driver. She had never been entitled to write it.

Sarah called before Emma could leave.

“Are you driving back tonight?”

“In a little while. I’ve found a possible lead.”

“Something we can use?”

“Not in print. Not yet.”

“Good,” Sarah said. “I’d rather have a verified fact tomorrow than an interesting mistake tonight.”

After the call, Emma opened the scanned material from her 2011 reporting. Searching for Reid returned several results. One appeared in a programme for an August event organised by the Glenarraidh Education Trust. Under Community volunteers was the name Daniel Reid.

Emma studied the document. A name on a programme could establish that somebody had been listed, but not that he had attended the event, owned a particular car or helped Claire leave. It did not even establish that this Daniel Reid was the man Nora remembered.

She drafted a small list of checks: the hall’s old booking records, the trust’s volunteer registers, and any contemporary photograph with a readable number plate. She would also need to ask Nora, through James, whether the first name Daniel meant anything to her. She would not call Nora again without permission.

A second document caught her attention: a surviving index of the trust’s committee meetings. The entries ran regularly through the summer of 2011, then stopped before September. There might be an ordinary explanation. The file could be incomplete; older minutes might be held elsewhere.

Emma wrote gap in archive — reason unknown.

Her phone lit up with a message from a number she did not recognise.

Ask why the trust stopped keeping its old meeting records.

For a moment the words seemed almost too well timed. Someone apparently knew what she was examining. But the message contained no evidence that its sender had seen her screen, nor that the trust had actually stopped keeping records. It might have been based on public information or a guess.

Emma saved the message, including the time and number, and forwarded it to Sarah without attaching a theory.

Then she started the engine. As the wipers cleared the glass, the village road came into view. She had a name to verify, a break in an archive to investigate, and an anonymous message that could mean something—or nothing at all.
